title: NATO Drafts Plan to Defeat a Russian Attack With Drones and AI
source_used: The Straits Times (carries Bloomberg's own text, credited BLOOMBERG); cross-checked with ThePrint's auto-generated Bloomberg copy, which has the same text
key_facts: NATO's top military commander, Supreme Allied Commander Europe US General Alexus Grynkewich, is working on a 'theory of victory' strategy for a quick win against a Russian attack on NATO's eastern flank, built around integrating drones and AI into traditional forces.
Bloomberg has seen the document in unclassified form; Grynkewich is due to present it in Poland on 12 Oct 2026, amid heightened NATO-Russia tensions.
It is meant to clarify how the alliance would handle a possible incursion into NATO territory, according to senior officials and diplomats speaking anonymously.

If NATO were attacked, it would block an incursion with land forces and assets from the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative (low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems, AI-enabled targeting), then destroy enemy command and control to defeat Russian forces quickly and overwhelmingly.
The strategy insists NATO is defensive, avoids unintended provocation and names hybrid threats (hostile acts below the level of open conflict) as part of deterrence.

Grynkewich's spokesman, Colonel Martin O'Donnell, declined to discuss details but called the alliance 'purely defensive'; NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has said there are no signs Russia is preparing a conventional attack.

The document is also meant to reassure the public, show allies how NATO would combine traditional weapons with the new capabilities that have emerged since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and urge more defence investment; allies are debating how to split spending between traditional weapons such as tanks and new technology.

The US sent allies a questionnaire this summer on defence spending and support for President Trump's policies, ahead of planned cuts to US military assets in Europe, and asked if allies could commit more forces to Grynkewich's plans.
quote_evidence: NATO's top military commander is working on a strategy for achieving a quick victory against a Russian attack on its eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defence technologies like drones and AI into traditional power.

The so-called theory of victory document, which Bloomberg has seen in an unclassified form, will be presented by Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, in Poland on Oct 12 amid heightened tensions between NATO and Russia.
Grynkewich spokesman Colonel Martin O'Donnell declined to discuss details of the plan, but emphasised that the alliance was "purely defensive."
why_it_matters_hint: The document is meant to show allies what forces and technology NATO would rely on and to push more defence spending, while the alliance weighs tanks against drones and AI.
